segments.title: HMAS Geranium's rapid 1915 build
segments.summary: HMAS Geranium was an Arabis-class sloop laid down in August and launched on 8 November 1915, only a few months later.
segments.body: HMAS Geranium was a Scottish-built Arabis-class sloop. Her keel was laid in August 1915, and she was launched on 8 November. The gap of only a few months between those milestones makes the speed of her wartime construction clear. The opening dates establish how little time this particular First World War hull spent on the stocks.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Geranium's class, Scottish construction, August 1915 laying down, and 8 November launch.

segments.title: From Royal Navy sloop to Australian hulk
segments.summary: Follow Geranium's transfer to Australia in 1919, decommissioning in 1927, and final disposal as a sunken hulk in 1935.
segments.body: Geranium transferred from Royal Navy service to Australia in 1919 and remained in Australian hands until she was decommissioned in 1927. The transferred wartime hull therefore had a substantial postwar career. She was dismantled in 1932 and sunk as a hulk in 1935. Her disposal happened in stages rather than at decommissioning or immediately after the armistice.

evidence.note: The transcript dates Geranium's Australian transfer, decommissioning, dismantling, and sinking as a hulk.

segments.title: Range and coal in a 1,250-ton sloop
segments.summary: At 1,250 tons, Geranium could make 16.5 knots and cover about 2,000 nautical miles at 15 knots on 250 tons of coal.
segments.body: Geranium displaced 1,250 tons and measured 267 feet 9 inches long, 33 feet 6 inches wide, with a draft of 11 feet 9 inches. Her top speed was 16.5 knots, and at 15 knots she could travel about 2,000 nautical miles. Achieving that range required 250 tons of coal. The figures show how tightly speed, endurance, and fuel supply were linked aboard a small coal-fired warship.

evidence.note: The transcript lists displacement, dimensions, speed, range, and the 250-ton coal load.

segments.title: More personnel for a growing Australian navy
segments.summary: Geranium's complement rose from 77 in the Royal Navy to 113 in Australian service as the RAN used transferred ships to expand.
segments.body: Geranium carried a complement of 77 in Royal Navy service and 113 after transfer to the Royal Australian Navy. The larger Australian complement reflected the use of these ships to grow the service and its pool of trained personnel. Her gun fit included two quick-firing 4-inch Mark IV guns in single mounts, later replaced by 4.7-inch Mark IV guns, plus two 3-pounders. The manning and armament details show that acquiring the hull was only one part of expanding naval capacity.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the two complements, explains the RAN's growth, and describes the gun fit.

segments.title: Converting Geranium for hydrographic survey
segments.summary: The Royal Australian Navy removed Geranium's weapons, installed survey equipment, and used her as its first survey vessel with a Fairey III aboard.
segments.body: Geranium entered Australian service in a survey role rather than as an armed sloop. Her weapons were removed to make room for survey equipment, changing both her fit and her operational purpose. She became the Royal Australian Navy's first survey vessel and carried a Fairey III seaplane. Shipborne survey gear and aviation gave the former sloop a markedly different purpose from her original armed service.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the Fairey III, the removal of weapons, survey equipment, and Geranium's first-survey-vessel role.

segments.title: A North Sea design in tropical survey waters
segments.summary: A sloop designed for North Sea conditions struggled in tropical Australian waters and grounded off Vanderlin Island and in the McArthur River.
segments.body: Geranium's conversion did not erase the limitations of her original design. Built for a North Sea climate, she did not work well in tropical waters. She grounded on an uncharted reef off Vanderlin Island and also in the McArthur River. For a survey ship, those incidents make the mismatch between design environment and operating area especially clear.

evidence.note: The transcript links tropical operating difficulties to the North Sea design and names the grounding examples.

segments.title: Geranium assists the stranded Tasman
segments.summary: In 1924, after being fitted to carry a Fairey III, Geranium assisted the steamship Tasman when it struck a reef near Clark Island.
segments.body: Geranium was fitted to carry a Fairey III aircraft in 1924. She later assisted the steamship Tasman after it struck a reef off Clark Island. The incident brought several parts of her new role together: the former sloop carried a seaplane, worked around poorly charted waters, and supported another vessel in trouble. It is a compact example of how a survey ship could contribute to maritime assistance as well as charting.

evidence.note: The transcript says Geranium was fitted for a Fairey III in 1924 and assisted Tasman after the latter hit a reef off Clark Island.
